items.title: The cold chain's wider effect
items.claim: Mechanical refrigeration became common in 20th-century homes and supply chains. Beyond food preservation, what is one less-obvious effect?

options.text: It made beef cheaper to ship from Argentina to Europe, restructuring agriculture in both regions
It eliminated the need for canning

items.reveal:
Refrigerated ships from the 1880s onwards allowed Argentine, Australian and New Zealand meat exports to Britain, reshaping rural economies and diets.

Domestic refrigerators became common in US homes in the 1930s-1950s and in the UK from the 1960s.
items.why: Food technologies reorganise economies, not just kitchens.

items.title: Salt iodisation
items.claim: Iodised salt was introduced as a public health measure to address iodine deficiency. In which decade did it first reach mass deployment in the US?
items.reveal:
Iodised salt was introduced commercially in Michigan in 1924, addressing goitre in the 'goitre belt'.

WHO estimates universal salt iodisation has substantially reduced the global prevalence of iodine deficiency disorders since the 1990s.
items.why: Adding a micronutrient to a staple is among the most cost-effective public-health measures recorded.

items.title: Food miles vs diet choice
items.claim: Poore and Nemecek's 2018 Science analysis of food systems found transport accounts for what share of typical food carbon footprints?

options.text: Around 1-10% for most foods, with production stages dominating

items.reveal_title: Transport is usually a small slice; production dominates
items.reveal:
Poore and Nemecek (2018) aggregated data from over 38,000 farms. For most foods, on-farm emissions, land-use change and processing dominate. Air-freighted produce and beef from deforested land are exceptions.

Choosing what to eat typically dwarfs food miles for footprint.
items.why: Salient measures (miles travelled) can mislead about underlying impacts.
